subject: Anthropology
title: Megaliths
description: A micro-lesson that makes Megaliths usable.

hook.text: Stonehenge weighs 4,000 tons. No wheels, no cranes, no metal tools. How did they build it? And more: why?

buildup.text: Megaliths are large stone structures — standing stones, tombs, and circles — built by Neolithic communities.

discovery.text: They required organized labor, shared belief systems, and engineering knowledge far beyond simple farming.

twist.text: Megaliths weren't built by lost civilizations. Ordinary farming communities achieved extraordinary coordination.

climax.text: Megaliths prove that complex social organization existed long before cities, writing, or centralized states.

quiz.question: What do megaliths reveal about Neolithic societies?
options: They had complex social organization before states

details.summary: Megaliths are large stone structures — standing stones, stone circles, dolmens — built by prehistoric peoples worldwide. From Stonehenge to Göbekli Tepe, they demonstrate remarkable engineering capabilities and deep social organization among early communities.
details.whyItMatters: Megaliths show that complex social organization existed among pre-state societies. Stonehenge and Göbekli Tepe were built by people without metal tools, writing, or centralized government.
takeaways: Megaliths are large stone structures built by prehistoric peoples
They appear worldwide, from Europe to Asia to the Americas
Their construction implies complex social organization without states

faq.question: How were megaliths built without modern technology?
faq.answer: Communities used rollers, sledges, levers, ramps, and enormous collective labor. Experimental archaeology has shown that large groups using simple tools can move multi-ton stones. The challenge was social organization rather than technology.

faq.question: What purpose did megalithic structures serve?
faq.answer: Functions varied: astronomical observatories, burial monuments, ritual gathering places, territorial markers, and expressions of community identity. Göbekli Tepe was apparently a ritual site built before permanent settlements, inverting assumptions that religion followed civilization.
